contrast: *reassured* is how you feel; *reassuring* is the thing that causes it: *I felt reassured because her voice was reassuring*.

senses.gloss: No longer worried, because someone has taken your fear away.
examples: She felt *reassured* after talking to the doctor.
Everyone left the meeting *reassured* about their jobs.
I was *more reassured* by her calm tone than by anything she actually said.

contrast: The *-ing* form describes the thing that calms you; the *-ed* form describes the person: *a reassuring nurse*, *a reassured patient*.

senses.gloss: Making someone feel less worried or afraid.
examples: Her voice on the phone was calm and *reassuring*.
He gave the crowd a *reassuring* smile.
The nurse's explanation was far *more reassuring* than the leaflet.

senses.gloss: Refusing to obey rules or the people in charge.
examples: He was a *rebellious* teenager who skipped class all the time.
The students grew *more rebellious* as the new rules piled up.
There is something *rebellious* about the way she dresses.

senses.gloss: Changed so completely that it feels like a new life or a new start.
examples: After two weeks off, he felt completely *reborn*.
The old factory district has been *reborn* as an arts center.
The team looked *reborn* in the second half.

senses.gloss: Formal: stubbornly refusing to cooperate or obey.
examples: A few *recalcitrant* senators blocked the bill for a month.
The mule was *recalcitrant* and would not move.
He got *more recalcitrant* with every new rule the school added.

senses.gloss: Moving back and away from you, or slowly getting smaller.
examples: He is self-conscious about his *receding* hairline.
We watched the *receding* taillights disappear around the corner.
The *receding* floodwaters left mud across the whole street.

contrast: As an adjective it lives in a few fixed phrases — *received wisdom*, *received opinion*, *received ideas*. In *I received your email* it is just the verb.

senses.gloss: Generally accepted by most people, though not necessarily true.
examples: The *received* wisdom is that you should never put everything in one stock.
She spent her career challenging *received* ideas about diet.
That view has hardened into *received* opinion in the field.

senses.gloss: Happening or made a short time ago.
examples: In *recent* years the town has almost doubled in size.
Is there a *more recent* version of the report?
The damage is *recent* — it happened during last week's storm.

senses.gloss: Willing to listen to new ideas and think about them.
examples: The boss was surprisingly *receptive* to my idea.
Try to pitch it to a *receptive* audience first.
Voters are *more receptive* to the message than they were last year.

senses.gloss: Set back into a wall, ceiling or surface instead of sticking out.
examples: The kitchen has *recessed* lighting in the ceiling.
The door handle is *recessed* so nothing catches on it.
His eyes were dark and deeply *recessed*.

senses.gloss: Belonging to a period when the economy is shrinking.
examples: The economy is showing *recessionary* signs again.
Hiring freezes are a classic *recessionary* move.
Many firms cut travel in the *recessionary* years after 2008.

senses.gloss: Of a gene: showing up only when a child gets it from both parents.
examples: Blue eyes come from a *recessive* gene.
The trait is *recessive*, so both parents have to carry it.
Red hair is a *recessive* characteristic.

senses.gloss: Able to be filled with electricity again and used many times.
examples: The flashlight takes *rechargeable* batteries.
Is this battery *rechargeable*?
We switched to *rechargeable* AAs to save money.

senses.gloss: Given by each side to the other, in both directions.
examples: The two countries signed a *reciprocal* trade agreement.
Respect between a teacher and a student should be *reciprocal*.
Our states have a *reciprocal* deal on driver's licenses.

form: -less from an old verb *reck* — to care

senses.gloss: Acting without thinking about the danger or the damage.
examples: He was charged with *reckless* driving.
It would be *reckless* to spend the whole budget in January.
Her second husband was even *more reckless* with money than her first.

senses.gloss: Taken back and made usable again, especially old material or land.
examples: The table is made of *reclaimed* wood from an old barn.
Much of the airport sits on *reclaimed* land.
The water is *reclaimed* and used to irrigate the golf course.

senses.gloss: Living alone and avoiding other people.
examples: The *reclusive* author has not given an interview in thirty years.
He became *more reclusive* after his wife died.
She has grown quite *reclusive* in old age.

senses.gloss: Easy to know again when you see or hear it.
examples: Her voice is instantly *recognizable*.
He wore a hat, but his walk was still *recognizable*.
The logo is one of the *most recognizable* in the world.

comparison: not gradable — usually graded with *widely*: *a widely recognized expert*

senses.gloss: Officially accepted, or accepted by everyone as real or good.
examples: She is a *recognized* expert on immigration law.
The certificate is *recognized* by employers across the country.
Burnout is now a *recognized* medical condition.

senses.gloss: Having accepted something unwelcome that cannot be changed.
examples: She is *reconciled* to living alone.
He seems *reconciled* to the fact that he will never play again.
I am *more reconciled* to the move than I was in January.

senses.gloss: Friendly again after a quarrel.
examples: The brothers were finally *reconciled* after ten years of silence.
She hoped to be *reconciled* with her father before he died.

senses.gloss: Of surgery: rebuilding a part of the body that was damaged.
examples: She had *reconstructive* surgery after the accident.
He is a *reconstructive* surgeon at the children's hospital.
Insurance covered the *reconstructive* work but not the cosmetic part.

senses.gloss: Better or bigger than anything of its kind before.
examples: She swam a *record-breaking* time in the 200 meters.
The movie had a *record-breaking* opening weekend.
It was a *record-breaking* heat wave for July.

senses.gloss: Captured on tape, video or a computer so it can be played later.
examples: They played *recorded* music instead of hiring a band.
This call may be *recorded* for training purposes.
He left a *recorded* message for the whole staff.

senses.gloss: Written down in an official record.
examples: It was the warmest June in *recorded* history.
There is no *recorded* case of the disease in this state.

senses.gloss: Able to be got back after being lost, spent or deleted.
examples: Deleted files are usually *recoverable* for about thirty days.
Only part of the loss is *recoverable* through insurance.
The data on the burned drive was not *recoverable*.

senses.gloss: Healthy again after an illness or injury.
examples: She is fully *recovered* from the surgery.
He looks *recovered*, but he still tires by noon.

senses.gloss: Found and brought back after being lost or stolen.
examples: Police returned the *recovered* jewelry to its owner.
The *recovered* files filled three hard drives.

position: attributive only — after a verb it is the verb *recover*, not an adjective: *She is recovering well*
contrast: A *recovering* alcoholic keeps the *-ing* form for life — *recovered* would suggest the problem is over and gone.

senses.gloss: Getting better after an illness, an injury or an addiction.
examples: He is a *recovering* alcoholic and has been sober for six years.
The ward has a quiet lounge for *recovering* patients.
She counsels *recovering* addicts at a community center.

senses.gloss: Done for fun in your free time, not for work or medical need.
examples: The town is building a new *recreational* center by the lake.
*Recreational* marijuana is legal in several states.
He plays *recreational* soccer on Sunday mornings.

senses.gloss: Medical: of or through the rectum.
examples: The nurse took a *rectal* temperature.
He is scheduled for a *rectal* exam next week.
The medicine comes as a *rectal* suppository.

contrast: *recurrent* and *recurring* mean nearly the same thing; *recurring* is the everyday word and *recurrent* is the one doctors and critics use.

senses.gloss: Coming back again and again over a long time.
examples: She has a *recurrent* dream about missing a train.
Back pain has been a *recurrent* problem for him since the fall.
The theme is *recurrent* throughout the novel.

senses.gloss: Happening again and again, often on a set schedule.
examples: Set up a *recurring* payment so you do not forget the rent.
It is a *recurring* joke on the show.
She has had *recurring* headaches since the concussion.

senses.gloss: Able to be treated and used again instead of thrown away.
examples: Put all *recyclable* materials in the blue bin.
Is this container *recyclable*?
Most glass and aluminum is *recyclable*.

contrast: Usually said of men and often half-joking. It means full of energy and ordinary appetites, not angry or violent.

senses.gloss: Full of healthy energy and normal desires.
examples: He is a *red-blooded* American teenager.
No *red-blooded* fan would miss that game.
It is the kind of movie that appeals to *red-blooded* action lovers.

form: compound — color + noun, from the carpet rolled out for important guests

senses.gloss: Grand and ceremonious, the way important guests are welcomed.
examples: They gave the visiting team the *red-carpet* treatment.
He got a *red-carpet* welcome at the airport.
It was a *red-carpet* reception, complete with photographers.

comparison: not gradable — usually intensified with *very* or *increasingly*

senses.gloss: Embarrassed, especially in public.
examples: The mayor was left *red-faced* when the numbers turned out to be wrong.
A *red-faced* official admitted the mistake to reporters.

senses.gloss: With a red face from anger, heat or hard effort.
examples: He came in *red-faced* and out of breath.
The coach was *red-faced* with rage by halftime.

position: predicative only — almost always after *catch*: *caught red-handed*
form: compound — color + noun + *-ed*, from the image of blood on a killer's hands
contrast: It lives in one phrase, *catch someone red-handed*, and never goes before a noun.

senses.gloss: In the act of doing something wrong, so there is no denying it.
examples: The guard caught him *red-handed* with the cash in his pocket.
They were caught *red-handed* copying answers off a phone.
If you take it, you will get caught *red-handed*.

senses.gloss: Heated until the metal glows red.
examples: He pulled the *red-hot* iron out of the fire with tongs.
Do not touch the burner — it is *red-hot*.

senses.gloss: Very exciting, very successful or very much in demand right now.
examples: She is the *red-hot* favorite for the award.
The company's stock was *red-hot* all last quarter.

position: attributive only — almost always in *a red-letter day*
form: compound — from the red ink that marked feast days on old calendars

senses.gloss: Of a day: important and happy, one you will remember.
examples: The day she got her citizenship was a *red-letter* day.
Graduation is a *red-letter* day for the whole family.
Mark it on the calendar — it is a *red-letter* day around here.

comparison: not gradable — the *-ish* ending already means somewhat

senses.gloss: Slightly red, or red mixed with another color.
examples: She has *reddish* hair and very pale skin.
The sky over the desert turned a *reddish* orange.
The soil here is *reddish* and full of clay.

form: compound — two colors joined with a hyphen

senses.gloss: Brown with a clear touch of red in it.
examples: The dog has a thick *reddish-brown* coat.
The leaves turn a deep *reddish-brown* in late October.
The stain on the carpet was *reddish-brown* and would not come out.

takes: *for* + what you get; *at* + where you use it

senses.gloss: Able to be exchanged for goods, money or a service.
examples: The coupon is *redeemable* for one free coffee.
These points are *redeemable* at any partner hotel.
The voucher is *redeemable* in store only.

position: attributive only — almost always with *quality*, *feature* or *value*

senses.gloss: Good enough to make up for everything that is bad about something.
examples: The movie's one *redeeming* quality is the soundtrack.
He has no *redeeming* features that I can see.
The apartment is tiny, but the view is its *redeeming* feature.

senses.gloss: Saving someone from guilt or failure, and giving them a second chance.
examples: The novel ends on a *redemptive* note.
He sees his volunteer work as *redemptive*.
There is a *redemptive* quality to the final scene.

contrast: The person is *a redhead* (noun); the adjective keeps the *-ed*: *a redheaded kid*.

senses.gloss: Having red or orange hair.
examples: A *redheaded* boy answered the door.
Both of her kids are *redheaded*.
He is the *redheaded* one in the back row.

contrast: It means formidable and worth respecting. It has nothing to do with *doubt*, even though it looks like it.

senses.gloss: Strong and impressive enough to be worth fearing or respecting.
examples: She faced a *redoubtable* opponent in the final.
The *redoubtable* Mrs. Hayes ran the office for forty years.
He proved a *more redoubtable* negotiator than anyone expected.

senses.gloss: Made smaller, lower or cheaper than before.
examples: The store sells last season's coats at *reduced* prices.
Students pay a *reduced* fare on the city bus.
He works a *reduced* schedule while he finishes his degree.

contrast: In British English *made redundant* means laid off from a job. Americans do not use it that way — they say *laid off*.

senses.gloss: Repeating something that has already been said, and so not needed.
examples: Saying free gift is *redundant* — a gift is already free.
Cut the second paragraph; it is *redundant*.
The report gets *more redundant* with every draft.

senses.gloss: Built in twice on purpose, as a backup.
examples: The plane has *redundant* control systems.
Customer data is stored on *redundant* servers in two states.

senses.gloss: Polite, cultured and in good taste.
examples: She has beautifully *refined* manners.
His taste in music is *more refined* than mine.

senses.gloss: Made pure by industrial processing.
examples: Try to cut back on *refined* sugar and white flour.
*Refined* oil is shipped by rail from the coast.

senses.gloss: Improved by many small careful changes.
examples: The second version of the design is far *more refined*.
We use a *refined* version of the original formula.

senses.gloss: Thinking quietly and seriously about things.
examples: He was in a *reflective* mood all evening.
The last chapter is calm and *reflective*.
She has grown *more reflective* with age.

senses.gloss: Throwing back light, so it can be seen in the dark.
examples: Runners should wear a *reflective* vest at night.
The jacket has *reflective* stripes down the sleeves.

senses.gloss: Showing what something is really like, or being a sign of it.
examples: The test scores are *reflective* of the whole district.
His answer was *reflective* of a much deeper problem.

senses.gloss: Done automatically, without stopping to think.
examples: His *reflexive* answer was no, and he regretted it later.
She has a *reflexive* distrust of salespeople.

senses.gloss: Grammar: pointing back to the subject of the verb.
examples: *Myself* and *herself* are *reflexive* pronouns.
In he hurt himself, the verb takes a *reflexive* pronoun.

senses.gloss: Wanting to change a system to make it work better.
examples: A *reform-minded* mayor took office last year.
The new board is *more reform-minded* than the old one.
*Reform-minded* teachers pushed for a longer school day.

senses.gloss: No longer doing the bad thing you used to do.
examples: He is a *reformed* smoker and now hates the smell.
She is a *reformed* shoplifter who counsels teenagers.

senses.gloss: Of a system or law: changed so that it works better.
examples: The *reformed* tax code takes effect in January.
Critics say the *reformed* system is no fairer than the old one.

contrast: The same word is also a noun: *a reformist* is a person who wants reform.

senses.gloss: Supporting gradual change to a political or religious system.
examples: The *reformist* wing of the party won the vote.
He ran on a *reformist* platform and lost badly.
*Reformist* candidates did well in the big cities.

contrast: *refreshed* is how you feel; *refreshing* is what causes it: *a refreshing nap leaves you refreshed*.

senses.gloss: Rested and full of energy again.
examples: I woke up *refreshed* for the first time in weeks.
A twenty-minute nap left her feeling *refreshed*.
He came back from vacation *more refreshed* than anyone expected.

takes: *to*-infinitive, after *it*: *It is refreshing to hear that*

senses.gloss: Cool and pleasant, making you feel less hot or tired.
examples: A glass of cold lemonade is *refreshing* on a day like this.
We took a *refreshing* swim in the lake before dinner.

senses.gloss: Pleasantly different from the usual, in a way you welcome.
examples: It is *refreshing* to hear a politician admit a mistake.
Her honesty was *more refreshing* than anything else that week.

senses.gloss: Kept cold so that it does not spoil.
examples: The vaccine has to travel in a *refrigerated* truck.
Keep the dough *refrigerated* until you are ready to bake.
The store added a whole *refrigerated* section for drinks.

contrast: *regal* describes a manner that reminds you of a king (*a regal wave*); *royal* says the person or thing really belongs to a king's family (*the royal family*).

senses.gloss: Grand and dignified, like a king or queen.
examples: She has a *regal* bearing that people notice right away.
The old hotel looks *more regal* from the street than it does inside.
He gave a *regal* nod and walked past us.

senses.gloss: Organized by strict rules and a strict schedule, often too strict.
examples: Her day is highly *regimented*, down to the minute.
He grew up in a *regimented* household with a chore chart.
Training camp is *more regimented* than the regular season.

senses.gloss: Belonging to one part of a country rather than the whole of it.
examples: The chain started as a small *regional* grocery in Ohio.
She won the *regional* championship in March.
There are *regional* differences in how people say that word.

senses.gloss: Officially listed, licensed or recorded.
examples: She is a *registered* nurse at the county hospital.
You have to be a *registered* voter to take part.
The name is a *registered* trademark.

senses.gloss: Of a tax or fee: taking a bigger share from people who earn less.
examples: A sales tax is *regressive* because it hits poor families hardest.
Critics call the flat fee deeply *regressive*.

senses.gloss: Going back to an earlier and worse state.
examples: The policy is a *regressive* step for women's rights.
His behavior got *more regressive* the longer he stayed home.

contrast: *regretful* is how a person feels; *regrettable* is a thing that is a shame: *a regretful apology* for *a regrettable mistake*.

senses.gloss: Feeling sorry about something you did or missed.
examples: She sounded *regretful* about missing the wedding.
He gave a *regretful* shrug and closed the door.
The older he gets, the *more regretful* he seems about that year.

senses.gloss: Bad enough that people are sorry it happened.
examples: The whole incident was *regrettable* but nobody's fault.
He made a *regrettable* remark about her weight.
It is *regrettable* that no one spoke up sooner, and even *more regrettable* that no one has apologized.

senses.gloss: Happening again and again at even intervals.
examples: Take the medicine at *regular* intervals, about six hours apart.
Her heartbeat is strong and *regular* now.
His visits have become *more regular* since he retired.

senses.gloss: Normal or standard, not special and not large.
examples: I will just have a *regular* coffee, nothing fancy.
It is not a holiday — it is a *regular* workday.

senses.gloss: Coming to the same place or doing the same thing often.
examples: He is one of our *regular* customers.
The bar has a few *regular* patrons who come every night.

senses.gloss: Grammar: following the normal pattern.
examples: *Walk* is a *regular* verb — its past is *walked*.
Most English plurals are *regular* and simply add an s.

senses.gloss: Controlled by official rules.
examples: Banking is a heavily *regulated* industry.
The market is *more regulated* now than it was in 2005.
Water quality is closely *regulated* by the state.

senses.gloss: Having to do with official rules and the bodies that enforce them.
examples: The merger still faces a *regulatory* review.
*Regulatory* agencies have been slow to act.
There are a few *regulatory* hurdles to clear first.

contrast: Spelled from *reign* (to rule), not *raining* or *reining*, though all three sound the same.

senses.gloss: Holding the title or the throne right now.
examples: She is the *reigning* world champion.
The *reigning* monarch opened parliament on Tuesday.
He is the *reigning* king of late-night television.

senses.gloss: Made stronger by adding extra material or support.
examples: The bunker is built of *reinforced* concrete.
The backpack has *reinforced* straps at the shoulders.
The door was *reinforced* with steel plates.

senses.gloss: Turned down or refused.
examples: He keeps a folder of *rejected* drafts.
*Rejected* applicants can appeal within thirty days.

senses.gloss: Feeling unwanted by other people.
examples: She felt hurt and *rejected* after that phone call.
Kids who feel *rejected* by classmates often act out.

senses.gloss: Computing: storing data in tables that are linked to each other.
examples: The app runs on a *relational* database.
SQL was built for *relational* data.

senses.gloss: Having to do with how people get along with each other.
examples: The therapist focuses on *relational* problems rather than symptoms.
Teaching has a strong *relational* side that no test measures.

contrast: The same word is also a common noun: *a relative* is a member of your family.

senses.gloss: Judged by comparison with something else, not on its own.
examples: After the storm, the *relative* calm felt strange.
They live in *relative* comfort compared with their neighbors.
What counts as expensive is *relative* to how much you earn.

senses.gloss: Grammar: joining a clause to the noun it describes.
examples: *Who*, *which* and *that* introduce a *relative* clause.
*Whose* is a *relative* pronoun.

form: -less from *relent* — to soften or give in

senses.gloss: Never stopping or easing off.
examples: The *relentless* heat lasted the whole of August.
The pressure on young athletes is *relentless*.

senses.gloss: Refusing to give up or to show any mercy.
examples: She is *relentless* once she decides she wants something.
Their defense got *more relentless* in the fourth quarter.

senses.gloss: Connected with the subject at hand, and therefore worth considering.
examples: Please bring any *relevant* documents to the meeting.
That question is not *relevant* to what we are discussing.
The book feels *more relevant* now than when it came out.

senses.gloss: Able to be trusted to do what is needed, every time.
examples: She is the *most reliable* person on the team.
We need a *more reliable* car for that drive.

senses.gloss: Of information: likely to be correct.
examples: Is that a *reliable* source?
We have *reliable* figures for only three of the years.

position: predicative only — before a noun only inside compounds like *self-reliant*

senses.gloss: Needing someone or something in order to manage.
examples: The town is heavily *reliant* on summer tourism.
He has become *more reliant* on his phone than he would like.
Many older residents are *reliant* on the one bus line.

senses.gloss: Glad because something you were worried about is over or did not happen.
examples: I am so *relieved* that you are okay.
She gave a *relieved* laugh when the test came back clean.
He looked *more relieved* than happy when the verdict was read.

senses.gloss: Believing in a religion and practicing it.
examples: Her family is very *religious* and goes to church twice a week.
He became *more religious* after his illness.

senses.gloss: Having to do with religion.
examples: The museum has a whole room of *religious* art.
*Religious* holidays are marked on the school calendar.

senses.gloss: Still there after the rest has gone or been used.
examples: Divide the *remaining* money between the two of you.
The *remaining* guests stayed to help clean up.
We will deal with the *remaining* questions tomorrow.

senses.gloss: Unusual enough that people notice and talk about it.
examples: She has made a *remarkable* recovery.
The house is *remarkable* for its stained-glass windows.
What is *most remarkable* is how calm he stayed.

senses.gloss: Of a class: teaching the basics to students who are behind.
examples: He had to take *remedial* math his freshman year.
The district pays for *remedial* reading classes.

senses.gloss: Meant to put right something that has gone wrong.
examples: The city took *remedial* action after the flood.
*Remedial* work on the bridge starts Monday.

position: predicative only — after *be* or *seem*, almost always with *of*

senses.gloss: Making you think of someone or something else.
examples: The smell was *reminiscent* of my grandmother's kitchen.
Her singing is *reminiscent* of early Joni Mitchell.
The lobby is *more reminiscent* of a hotel than an office.

position: predicative only — after *be*, often in *It would be remiss of me not to...*

senses.gloss: Formal: careless about a duty you should have carried out.
examples: It would be *remiss* of me not to thank the volunteers.
The inspector was *remiss* in not checking the wiring.
I would be *remiss* if I did not mention her help.

senses.gloss: Feeling deep guilt about something bad you did.
examples: He seemed genuinely *remorseful* about what he had done.
The judge saw no sign of a *remorseful* defendant.
She grew *more remorseful* as the details came out in court.

senses.gloss: Feeling no guilt at all about the harm you cause.
examples: The killer was cold and *remorseless* on the stand.
He seemed *more remorseless* with every question the prosecutor asked.

senses.gloss: Never letting up.
examples: The *remorseless* rain went on for five days.
There is a *remorseless* logic to her argument.

comparison: -er/-est or more/most — *remoter* or *more remote*, *remotest* or *most remote*

senses.gloss: Far away from towns and from other people.
examples: They live on a *remote* island off the coast of Maine.
The cabin was *more remote* than the photos suggested.

senses.gloss: Done from home or from another city instead of at the office.
examples: The job is fully *remote*, with two trips a year.
She has had a *remote* position since 2020.

senses.gloss: Of a chance or possibility: very small.
examples: There is not the *remotest* chance he will agree.
The risk is *remote* but it is real.

senses.gloss: Distant and hard to get close to, in manner.
examples: He can seem *remote* until you know him well.
Her father was a *remote* figure throughout her childhood.

senses.gloss: Operated from a distance by a handheld device or a signal.
examples: He got a *remote-controlled* car for his birthday.
The gate is *remote-controlled*, so stay in the truck.
They filmed the wedding with a *remote-controlled* drone.

senses.gloss: Made so it can be taken off and put back.
examples: The stroller has a *removable* seat cover you can wash.
The stickers are *removable* and will not damage the paint.
It comes with a *removable* liner for cold weather.

position: after the noun — in *a first cousin once removed*; otherwise after a verb, in *far removed from*
contrast: In *a cousin once removed*, *removed* means one generation apart — nobody was taken away.

senses.gloss: Very different or very distant from something.
examples: His account of the evening is far *removed* from what actually happened.
Life in the capital is far *removed* from village life.

senses.gloss: Of a cousin: one or two generations apart from you.
examples: She is my first cousin once *removed*.
He is a cousin twice *removed* on my mother's side.

contrast: The same word is also a noun: *a renegade* is the person who breaks away.

senses.gloss: Having left the group you belonged to and turned against it.
examples: A *renegade* group broke away from the main party.
The movie is about a *renegade* cop who ignores every rule.
*Renegade* soldiers seized the radio station at dawn.

senses.gloss: Of energy or resources: never running out, because nature replaces it.
examples: The state gets a third of its power from *renewable* sources.
Wind and solar are *renewable*; coal is not.

senses.gloss: Able to be extended for another period of time.
examples: The contract is for one year, *renewable* for two more.
Your permit is *renewable* online in about ten minutes.

senses.gloss: Starting again, and often stronger than before.
examples: There is *renewed* interest in the case after the documentary.
She came back from the break with *renewed* energy.
*Renewed* fighting broke out near the border.

senses.gloss: Famous and widely admired for something good.
examples: He is one of the *most renowned* heart surgeons in the country.
The region is *renowned* for its wine.
She is *renowned* as a teacher as much as a performer.

contrast: The same form works as an adverb after a verb — *They lived there rent-free* — and that use is not an adjective.

senses.gloss: Costing nothing to live in or use.
examples: They offered him a *rent-free* apartment above the shop.
The space is *rent-free* for the first six months.
The deal includes a *rent-free* period while the building is fixed up.

contrast: The same word is also a noun: *a rental* is the car or apartment you have rented.

senses.gloss: Rented out to people for money, or having to do with renting.
examples: We picked up the *rental* car at the airport.
*Rental* prices downtown have gone up again.
He owns three *rental* properties across the river.

senses.gloss: Able to be done again with the same result.
examples: An experiment has to be *repeatable* before anyone believes it.
We want a *repeatable* process, not one lucky quarter.

senses.gloss: Polite enough to say out loud.
examples: His reaction was not *repeatable* in front of the kids.
She said something about the referee that is not *repeatable* here.

contrast: *repeated* just says it happened more than once; *repetitive* adds that it is boringly the same.

senses.gloss: Happening more than once, again and again.
examples: *Repeated* warnings had no effect on him.
She made *repeated* attempts to reach the office by phone.
He was fired after *repeated* absences.

contrast: The same word is also a noun: *insect repellent* is the spray you put on your skin.

senses.gloss: So unpleasant that it makes you want to keep away.
examples: The whole idea is *repellent* to me.
He found the man's politics *more repellent* than his manners.

senses.gloss: Keeping a substance off, usually in a compound.
examples: The jacket is made of a water-*repellent* fabric.
The couch is treated with a stain-*repellent* coating.

senses.gloss: Sorry for what you did and wanting to make it right.
examples: He did not sound the least bit *repentant*.
A *repentant* thief returned the money anonymously.
She seemed *more repentant* once she saw the damage.

senses.gloss: Doing or saying the same thing over and over, usually in a boring way.
examples: The work is *repetitive* but it pays well.
Typing all day can cause *repetitive* strain injuries.
The second album is *more repetitive* than the first.

senses.gloss: Able to be swapped for a new one of the same kind.
examples: The battery is *replaceable*, so do not throw the whole thing out.
Everyone here is *replaceable* except the founder.
The filters are cheap and easily *replaceable*.

position: predicative only — after *be*, almost always with *with*
contrast: Formal and written. In speech Americans say *full of*.

senses.gloss: Filled with something, or having plenty of it.
examples: The report is *replete* with errors.
His speech was *replete* with quotations from the Bible.
The museum is *replete* with treasures from the region.
